title: Mathematical framework for simulation of non-perturbative cavity optomechanics with plate-like dielectrics
abstract: Cavity optomechanical models typically treat a sensor either as a perturbative polarizable object in a pre-existing optical field, or solve the field at a fixed equilibrium and linearize in a fixed optical-mode basis. Neither self-consistently determines the spatially resolved cavity field, the optical force, the mechanical equilibrium, and the back-action when a finite-thickness dielectric plate intercepts the entire optical mode and restructures the intracavity field. In this companion paper to [1], we develop that treatment by extending the vacuum two-photon formalism to finite-thickness planar dielectrics, incorporating their Fresnel reflection, internal propagation, optical forces, and mechanical back-action directly into the field equations. We derive the carrier and sideband transfer functions needed to describe the coupled optical-mechanical system, including optomechanical cooling and the response to external perturbations. The result is a systematic starting point for calculating detector response and noise budgets for cavity experiments with intracavity dielectrics, including gravitational wave detectors deploying levitated sensors.
summary: This paper develops a comprehensive, self-consistent mathematical framework for analyzing cavity optomechanics involving dielectric sensors. It overcomes limitations of previous models by treating the dielectric's field restructuring non-perturbatively. The resulting formalism allows for accurate calculation of optical forces and mechanical back-action, crucial for designing next-generation quantum detectors.
main_problem: The paper addresses the lack of a self-consistent mathematical framework for simulating cavity optomechanics when a finite-thickness dielectric plate significantly restructures the intracavity optical field.
main_result: A new formalism is developed that incorporates Fresnel reflection, internal propagation, optical forces, and mechanical back-action directly into the field equations, providing a systematic starting point for detector response calculations.
method: The methodology extends the vacuum two-photon formalism by solving the field evolution across free space, moving mirrors, and the dielectric slab using quadrature decomposition.
model_or_system: The system is a cavity containing a planar, levitated dielectric sensor. The model treats the interaction non-perturbatively, accounting for the dielectric's full optical response rather than assuming a fixed field basis.
key_observables: Carrier and sideband transfer functions, optical forces (DC and AC), mechanical back-action, and the total noise budget for detector response.
important_parameters: Dielectric thickness ($L_s$), cavity length ($L_c$), trap laser power ($P_{	ext{trap}}$), and the sensor's refractive index ($n$).
main_assumptions: The model assumes fields are well-described by plane waves propagating between surfaces of infinite areal extent aligned with the cavity axis, and that all optics are lossless.
figures_summary: Fig. 1 shows the basic setup with two coaxial lasers and the dielectric sensor. Fig. 3 illustrates the field entering, propagating within, and leaving the moving dielectric slab.
paper_structure: The paper builds the framework by first defining the field evolution across different optical elements (free space, moving mirrors, dielectric slab) using the two-photon formalism, leading to self-consistent calculations of forces and back-action.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it provides advanced theoretical tools for modeling quantum light-matter interactions in complex, non-linear optical cavities, which is central to modern quantum sensing and cavity QED.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Basic diagram of a plate-like levitated sensor trapped within a cavity. A spatially similar trap and probe beam, with powers Ptrap and Pprobe, respectively, enter the cavity of length Lc from the left. The planar sensor, with thickness Ls, is trapped a distance Lt away from the input mirror. Darker red shades indicate greater laser intensities. The sensor’s cross section captures nearly the entire beam profile for both the trap and probe lasers at the trap location. The probe beam’s primary use is readout of the sensor position, but it also cools the sensor’s motion along the cavity axis.

FIG. 2. Schematic diagram of quadrature component vec- tors for (left) a free space element of length L and (right) a moving mirror with amplitude reflectivity and transmissivity coefficients ρ and τ which is displaced from its mean position by a distance x ≪λ.

FIG. 3. Schematic diagram of the carrier and sideband fields entering, propagating within, and leaving a moving dielectric slab (gray) of length Ls which experiences displacement x(t). Field vector labels are chosen for comparison to Fig. 4.

FIG. 4. Diagram of the carrier and sideband fields in the cavity with a levitated dielectric. The labels for vectors describing the fields at various locations will be used in a number of calculations within Sec. I. The relative phase accumulated over free propagation elements for a laser with detuning ∆is written above the blue brackets.

FIG. 5. A set of transfer functions to the two quadratures of the reflected readout port. Here, we set the parameters Ls = 0.25λ/n and ∆= −0.5κ. Gray lines mark the trap resonant frequency (dotted) and new resonant frequency af- ter including the probe beam’s optical spring effect (dashed). Transfer function input ports include an external force (top), trap beam field fluctuations (middle), and probe beam field fluctuations (bottom). For the laser fluctuation entries, we only plot the response to a1 and a2 here because their ana- logues in p1 and p2 do not provide any noteworthy additional information.
